pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Elm trees are susceptible to a number of different anthracnose fungi, including Ophiognomonia intermedia , Gloeosporium betulae , Cryptocline betularum , and Cylindrosporium sp. Cryptocline is the fungus that we encounter the most frequently on samples submitted to the lab for diagnosis.

type_of_disease.quote: Elm trees are susceptible to a number of different anthracnose fungi

affected_parts.quote: Cryptocline is only known to colonize the leaves, so it overwinters in fallen leaf tissue.

summary.value: Leaf spots start as small, round chlorotic lesions that expand into necrotic spots with a purple/black border and tan or white center; large areas of the leaf blade turn yellow then necrotic before premature leaf drop.
summary.quote: Leaf spots may start as small, round chlorotic lesions that slowly expand over time (Figures 1 & 2). Eventually, a necrotic spot with a purple/black border and tan or white center will form (Figure 3).

diagnostic_features.value: Necrotic spot with a purple/black border and tan or white center; lesions developing on a leaf vein follow the vein creating a thin/elongate necrotic lesion instead of being circular; mature lesions are tan with black fungal structures (acervuli) within.
diagnostic_features.quote: Eventually, a necrotic spot with a purple/black border and tan or white center will form (Figure 3). Lesions may begin to develop on a leaf vein and instead of being circular will follow the vein a little, creating a thin necrotic lesion (Figure 4).

treatments.quote: Like other leaf spot pathogens that do not infect stems, removal of the foliage in the fall can reduce inoculum for the following year (though won't eliminate the disease). Providing fertilizer (where needed) and water (hot and dry periods) will help mitigate some tree stress, as stress can predispose plants to increased disease severity. Fungicides are not normally recommended for mature trees as it is impractical to get coverage across the entire canopy, but could be practical in a nursery setting if symptoms are observed and leading to leaf drop.

web_support.quote: Lesions of Cryptocline located on leaf veins create an elongate necrotic lesions instead of the typical round lesions located elsewhere on the leaf.
large lesions often follow leaf veins or are delimited by leaf veins.

deltas.image_shows: The leaf blade curls upward at the tip.
deltas.image_quote: The top right part of the leaf is curled upward.
deltas.reasoning: Leaf curling/cupping/distortion is documented for anthracnose (Cryptocline/Discula group), giving partial support, though sources note anthracnose typically causes downward rather than upward cupping so the direction is not firmly corroborated.

web_support.quote: Anthracnose is a common fungal disease of shade trees that results in leaf spots, cupping or curling of leaves and early leaf drop; infected leaves are often distorted, cupped or curled.
Young leaves become cupped or distorted with necrotic lesions.

dropped_contradictory.canonical_says: necrotic spots with a purple/black border and tan or white center
dropped_contradictory.image_shows: A lesion shows a concentric target-spot pattern with alternating light and dark rings.
dropped_contradictory.image_quote: A lesion with a concentric pattern showing a target spot with alternating light and dark rings.
dropped_contradictory.reasoning: Oak anthracnose (Cryptocline) lesions follow veins with a purple/black border and tan/white center; the concentric target/bull's-eye ring pattern is characteristic of other pathogens (e.g., Corynespora target spot), so external descriptions contradict this appearance for this disease.

web_support.quote: Large lesions often follow leaf veins or are delimited by leaf veins; old lesions are papery and gray to white in color.
Target spot lesions can result in a 'target' or bull's-eye pattern, though this is referenced in relation to a different fungal disease (Corynespora cassiicola) rather than typical oak anthracnose.

deltas.image_shows: Dead-tissue (necrotic) patterns are present on the foliage.
deltas.image_quote: Dead-tissue patterns (brown, black, bleached) are visible on the leaves.
deltas.reasoning: Leaf necrosis is indirectly consistent with the documented leaf scorch and blighted foliage of drippy blight, though the exact patterning is not diagnostic.

web_support.quote: Main symptoms on infected oaks are leaf scorch and premature leaf drop that is followed by dieback of small twigs and the development of branch cankers.
Disease symptoms such as fallen branches and blighted leaves are still present.

deltas.image_shows: A raised lesion suggests localized severity.
deltas.reasoning: Drippy blight is documented to form small lesions/twig cankers, giving partial support to a raised lesion, though the raised texture itself is not specifically described in sources.

web_support.quote: Trees inoculated on leaf whorls exhibited bacterial ooze within five to seven days of inoculation, with small lesions forming as the shoots elongated.
Twig cankers, indicated by maroon discoloration and clear margins, appear in the late summer near kermes-scale-feeding sites and wounds.

deltas.image_quote: The leaves show curling up towards the moth.
deltas.reasoning: Leaf curling is not among the documented drippy blight symptoms (ooze, dieback, maroon cankers) and no source corroborates it, but it is not directly contradicted.

deltas.image_shows: Leaf veins appear clear and translucent.
deltas.image_quote: The leaf veins are translucent and pale.
deltas.reasoning: Translucent leaf veins are not a documented drippy blight feature and no extension source corroborates it, but it is not contradicted.

deltas.image_shows: The leaf is spade-shaped with a broad base tapering to a point.
deltas.image_quote: The leaf has a broad base tapering to a point.
deltas.reasoning: This describes leaf outline rather than a disease sign, and no drippy blight source corroborates a symptom of this shape; left provisional as it is uncorroborated but not contradicted by disease literature.

deltas.image_shows: No chlorosis is evident in the imaged tissue.
deltas.image_quote: There are no visible signs of leaf blight.
deltas.reasoning: A negative observation of absent chlorosis/blight cannot be corroborated by published photo descriptions and is not contradicted, so it remains provisional.
